sources.title: Simone Veil (Q298180), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-18): English label 'Simone Veil', description 'French politician (1927-2017)', Korean label 시몬 베유, instance of human, born 13 July 1927, died 30 June 2017. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Judaica entry 'Veil, Simone' by Nelly Hansson (Gale, reproduced on Encyclopedia.com; read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: magistrate from 1956 and adviser in the Ministry of Justice who worked on reform of adoption, adult disability and parental authority law; minister of health in the Chirac government (1974-76) and of health and social security under Barre (1976-79), where she initiated the law legalising abortion; elected the first president of the directly elected European Parliament on 17 July 1979 (president to 1982, member to 1993); minister of social affairs in the Balladur government (1993-95); first president of the Foundation for the Memory of the Shoah. Reference-work biography, admiring in tone.

French National Assembly, 'Le dossier legislatif' for the 1975 abortion law (read in French): the bill was tabled on 15 November 1974, debated in the Assembly from 26 to 28 November, quotes members attacking it as 'barbarism' comparable to Nazi Germany and as embryos thrown into crematoria, records that she obtained a text only slightly amended, that the abortion provisions were adopted unchanged and the right to life reaffirmed in Article 1, and that the vote was 284 to 189, with most of the support coming from the opposition. The legislature's own record of the debate.

Laurence Coustal (AFP), 'Il y a un peu plus de 40 ans, le rude combat de Simone Veil en faveur de l'IVG', Public Senat, 30 June 2017 (read in French): a debate of more than 25 hours before an Assembly of 9 women and 481 men, her one-hour opening speech, named opponents and their language, 74 speakers, a vote of 284 to 189 in the night of 28-29 November 1974 in which two thirds of the governing majority voted against, and the five-year trial period made permanent in 1979. Quotes her 2004 interview book with Annick Cojean for her own reaction, so that part is self-report.

Jean-Marie Pottier, 'IVG: le jour ou Simone Veil a partage sa conviction de femme', Slate.fr, 30 June 2017 (read in French): context of the 1971 manifesto of the 343 and the Bobigny trials, the contents of the bill (decision left to the woman in the first ten weeks after a compulsory medical and social consultation and an eight-day reflection period, no reimbursement until 1982), extracts of her speech, the vote with only a third of the presidential majority in favour, and her own later view that the 1967 contraception law had mattered more. Independent journalism; her reactions again come from the Cojean interview.

Douglas Johnson, 'Simone Veil obituary', The Guardian, 30 June 2017 (read in full; the Irish Times obituary of the same date carries the same text and is not counted separately). A historian's obituary: her career as a magistrate (adviser to justice ministers, the Boupacha case, first woman secretary general of the magistrates' council in 1970, the 1969 adoption book), the three-day 1974 debate and the role of the opposition in passing the law, her other work as minister (medical-studies reform, an anti-smoking campaign described as largely unsuccessful, humane hospitals, organ-removal rules), her 1979 European Parliament list and presidency, her reluctance to commit to a party, and her opposition as a minister to wider state powers over immigration. Describes her as impatient and over-exacting. Camp deportation and bereavements are described there and are context only, not used for any row.

European Parliament Historical Archives, 'The Fonds of Simone Veil' (read in full, including the short biography and her own 'Reflections of Former Presidents' text): elected on 17 July 1979 by an absolute majority in the second round; the practical problems of the new directly elected assembly, the 1980 budget she declared adopted although it slightly exceeded the treaty ceiling, after which the French Government brought an action before the Court of Justice; her member-of-parliament posts to 1993. Institutional page; the reflections are her own account, so the budget episode is self-report.

'Profile: Simone Veil', Connexion France, 30 November 2016 (read in full): career summary with the political abuse she received in 1974, quotations from a review by the former UK minister Denis MacShane of her autobiography Une Vie about male resistance at each stage of her career (as a would-be magistrate and as a minister), a historian's remark on her European role, her election as the first woman president of the European Parliament, her seat on the Constitutional Council (1998-2007) and the Academie francaise (2008). Independent newspaper profile, admiring in tone.

Shoah Memorial (Paris), 'Tribute to Simone Veil, who died on 30 June 2017' (read in full): her career as an institution sees it, her roles at the Memorial of the Unknown Jewish Martyr, the Centre de Documentation Juive Contemporaine and, from 2001 to 2007, as first president of the Foundation for the Memory of the Shoah, and a 2005 speech asking that younger generations and political leaders be told how the genocide happened. Institutional tribute; used only for her public memorial roles, not for her wartime experience.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_veil_an, src_veil_ps, src_veil_slate, src_veil_guardian, src_veil_connexion | 1974 | parliamentary record, news-agency report, news magazine, historian's obituary, newspaper profile] In November 1974 she presented the abortion bill to an Assembly of 9 women and 481 men and stayed through three days of debate in which members, including some of her own majority, compared the bill to Nazi crimes (quoted in the Assembly's own dossier); two thirds of the governing majority voted against and the text passed with opposition votes. The conduct is recorded by independent sources; how she experienced it comes mostly from her own interview book, repeated by two of them. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 78 / 0.70 to 76 / 0.66 because the episode is one extended event and its inner stance rests on one self-report.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_veil_ej, src_veil_guardian, src_veil_connexion, src_veil_an, src_veil_epha | 1957-1995 | reference biography, historian's obituary, newspaper profile, parliamentary record, institutional archive] Documented reform work across several fields over four decades: adoption, disability and parental-authority law and prison conditions as a magistrate (a 1969 book on adoption), contraception and abortion law, medical-studies reform, hospital conditions and an anti-smoking campaign as minister, and later the European Parliament and memorial institutions. The sources describe what she worked on; none states her motives beyond her own memoir remarks.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_veil_guardian, src_veil_ps, src_veil_slate, src_veil_connexion | 1974-1995 | historian's obituary, news-agency report, news magazine, newspaper profile] She carried the abortion bill although two thirds of her own governing majority voted against it (though it was the president's project), is described as reluctant to commit to any party, and as a minister in 1993-95 opposed extending state powers to control immigration. Three separate episodes, mostly from one obituary, so the score stays moderate.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_veil_guardian, src_veil_ej, src_veil_connexion, src_veil_epha | 1957-1980 | historian's obituary, reference biography, newspaper profile, institutional archive] As a magistrate she brought a young woman held in an Algerian prison to safety in France and co-wrote a 1969 book on adoption with two doctors; as minister she reformed the medical-studies syllabus; as President of the European Parliament she declared the 1980 budget adopted despite its slightly exceeding the treaty ceiling, which led the French Government to go to the Court of Justice (her own account). Several of these were roles she was asked to take (the ministry and the European list were offered by the president), so the evidence for self-started action is partial.

persuasiveness.rationale: [src_veil_an, src_veil_slate, src_veil_guardian, src_veil_ps | 1974 | parliamentary record, news magazine, historian's obituary, news-agency report] The Assembly dossier says she obtained the abortion provisions unamended after a debate in which most support came from the opposition and a minority of the governing majority; the vote was 284 to 189. The outcome was shared with a president who insisted on the law and an opposition that endorsed it, and no source separates her speech from those factors. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.50 to 60 / 0.46 because the outcome is shared credit and a win by opposition votes is not direct evidence of her own persuasive effect.

persistence.rationale: [src_veil_connexion, src_veil_guardian, src_veil_ej | 1956-1979 | newspaper profile, historian's obituary, reference biography] The profile, quoting a review of her autobiography, says she had to overcome resistance at each stage of her career, beginning with her decision to become a magistrate (entered the magistracy in 1956); the obituary adds an anti-smoking campaign she continued although it was largely unsuccessful. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.50 to 62 / 0.46 because the claim leans on one review of her own memoir (source-family concentration) and the smoking campaign is a single line.

Sitter: the holder cataloguing as copied onto Commons gives 'Persoonsnaam: Veil, Simone', 'Simone Veil (Europees Parlement) bij uitreiking Four Freedoms Awards in Middelburg', 23 June 1984; the image has no lettering, so identity rests on catalogue data (other frames of the same event also show Queen Juliana, and the Stage B note says the holder title of the sibling frame names both; this restoration is a single-subject head and shoulders crop whose own title names Veil only); age and appearance are consistent with a woman in her mid-fifties.
